extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate discrete mathematics students and instructors (number theory/combinatorics)
extracted.subtask_description: A classroom-tested worksheet and project list about the linear Diophantine (Frobenius) problem for two or more generators, accompanied by solutions and classroom calculator activities for discrete mathematics. Includes theory (Euclidean algorithm consequences, Popoviciu’s formula), exercises (Questions 1–11), open projects, and TI-calculator activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation uniqueness (Question 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given relatively prime positive integers a and b, show that a given integer k can be uniquely written as k = m a + n b with m, n integers and 0 ≤ m < b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the basic uniqueness-of-remainder representation: use the Euclidean algorithm and the fact that adding/subtracting multiples of a and b yields all integral representations; choose the representative with the a-coefficient in [0,b-1].

rubrics_metrics.name: Representability criterion (Question 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterize when an integer k is representable as a nonnegative linear combination of a and b: write k = m a + n b with 0 ≤ m < b and conclude that k is representable iff n ≥ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the unique representation from Question 1. The constructive criterion (existence of m,n with m in [0,b-1] and n ≥ 0) gives a practical test for representability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiently large integers are representable (Questions 3 and 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For relatively prime a and b (and more generally for relatively prime a1,...,ad), every sufficiently large integer is representable as a nonnegative integer combination of the generators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For d=2 use the representability criterion of Question 2 to show a bound beyond which all integers are representable; for general d use the Euclidean algorithm existence of integer combinations and adjust coefficients into nonnegative ranges to conclude existence of a threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frobenius number formula for two generators (Question 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: For relatively prime positive integers a and b, the Frobenius number g(a,b) equals ab - a - b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maximize non-representable integers using the uniqueness/representability criterion from Question 2; a hint suggests trying to maximize integral coefficients subject to constraints 0 ≤ m < b and n < 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementary representability and Sylvester’s theorem (Questions 6 and 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: For 0 < k < ab not divisible by a or b, k is representable iff ab - k is not representable; deduce Sylvester’s theorem that the number of nonrepresentable integers equals 1/2 (a-1)(b-1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the representability characterization in Question 2 together with divisibility considerations; count integers in [1,ab] and apply the complementary property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting function rk and almost-periodicity (Question 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define rk as the number of representations of k as nonnegative combinations of a and b. Then rk+ab = rk + 1 (almost-periodicity identity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question 2 implies that increasing k by ab increases the number of representations by exactly one; note there is no analogous simple formula for d ≥ 3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric interpretation of rk (section)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret rk as counting integer lattice points on the line segment Lk (dilations of a fixed segment) in R^2; more generally, counts integer points in dilates of simplices for higher d (connections to Ehrhart theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the geometric picture to reason about growth/probability of integer points appearing on Lk and to motivate lattice-point enumeration techniques and Ehrhart-theoretic methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popoviciu’s explicit formula for rk (Theorem 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a and b are relatively prime, Popoviciu’s formula gives an explicit formula for rk in terms of k, ab, and fractional parts/modular inverses: rk = (k)/(ab) + 1 - {b^{-1} k / a} - {a^{-1} k / b}, where b^{-1} (mod a) and a^{-1} (mod b) are modular inverses and {·} is fractional part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem provides a closed formula for the representation-counting function rk; the text defines greatest-integer and fractional-part functions and notes generalizations exist but are more complex for d ≥ 3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications of Popoviciu: proofs of Frobenius properties (Questions 9 and 10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Popoviciu’s formula to (a) show that r_{ab} = 0 and r_{ab+n} > 0 for n > 0 (thus ab is the first representable beyond the Frobenius bound) and (b) derive complementary representability properties and Sylvester’s theorem as alternate proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use periodicity/behavior of fractional-part terms in Popoviciu’s formula and simple inequalities (e.g., floor/frac bounds) to reach the conclusions; hints reference periodicity of fractional part.

rubrics_metrics.name: j-representability and generalized Frobenius number gj (Question 11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define an integer k to be j-representable if it has exactly j representations; define gj as the largest j-representable integer. Prove properties: (a) gj is well-defined; (b) gj.j/ = ab - ⌈ab/j⌉ (?) (text gives explicit formula relationships); (c)-(e) give smallest j-representable integer, counts of uniquely representable integers, and counts of j-representable integers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use counting-function periodicity (Question 8), Popoviciu’s theorem, and arithmetic/translation arguments to deduce formulas and exact counts; parts are broken out (a)–(e) with hints about using periodicity and the formula for g(a,b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Project: New approach/algorithm for d ≥ 3 (Project 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research project: devise a new approach or algorithm for the Frobenius problem in cases with d ≥ 3 generators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes no easy formula analogous to d=2 and that Denham’s theorem gives computational tractability in some cases; project is open-ended and listed as hardest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project: Improved upper bounds for the Frobenius number (Project 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research project: develop improved upper bounds for the Frobenius number, building on known good lower bounds and several upper bounds in the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References cited (e.g., Davison, Ramírez-Alfonsín) provide starting points; recommended as research-level work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project: Vector (multi-dimensional) generalizations (Project 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research project: study vector generalizations of the Frobenius problem (multi-dimensional versions) which are largely unexplored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References [16,17] and Ehrhart-theoretic viewpoints may be relevant; suggested for exploratory research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project: Extend solved special cases (Project 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research project: identify and extend special solved cases of the Frobenius problem (e.g., arithmetic sequences) and find new special families where closed forms can be derived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey existing solved families (Ramírez-Alfonsín Chapter 3) and attempt to generalize or discover new tractable parameterizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project: Generalized Frobenius numbers gj (Project 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research project: study the generalized Frobenius numbers gj (from Question 11), derive formulas for special cases such as arithmetic sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine counting-function techniques, Popoviciu-style formulas, and combinatorial enumeration to obtain explicit results for gj in concrete families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design goals for calculator activities (summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculator activities should (1) enhance discrete-math understanding, (2) help transition students from concrete computation to abstract reasoning, (3) require students to interpret calculator output rather than depend on it to 'prove', and (4) encourage experimentation and discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor notes recommend demonstrations in class to ensure correct usage, activities that ask for interpretation of output, and tasks aiming to reduce student dependency on calculators as black boxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity 1: Modular arithmetic (TI-89 requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce and explore the mod function graphically (y = a mod n) on the TI-89; students graph sequences, trace values, and interpret congruence classes visually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TI-83+/TI-84+ lack a native mod n function (activity not supported on those without adaptation). Instructions specify sequence mode, example windows, tracing to collect values, and solving simultaneous congruences graphically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity 2: Calculator-aided conjecture and counterexample (Help with proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use calculators to experiment, conjecture, and find counterexamples for proof exercises (e.g., parity of n^2−1, divisibility conjectures); item 5 requires TI-89 symbolic nCr capability for exploring combinatorial identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize that calculators cannot prove statements: they are tools to test, generate examples, and find counterexamples. Some items can be done on any calculator; symbolic/combinatorial items need TI-89 capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity 3: Floor and ceiling functions (graphical exploration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Graph and analyze floor and ceiling functions, their compositions, sums, and discontinuities; determine intervals of continuity and endpoint inclusion, and adapt exercises for TI-83/84 using int(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put calculators in dot mode, use appropriate menus for floor/ceiling, ask students to identify discontinuities and differences between step and diagonal graphs; require attention to included endpoints on graphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity 4: Growth of functions, big-O and little-o (graphical experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use graphing calculators to visualize asymptotic growth, test big-O/o relations, graph ratios and limits to judge relative growth rates, and find constants C,k for O-notation by experimenting with windows and scaling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples (polynomials vs logs/exponentials), graph ratios to infer limits (supporting use of L’Hôpital in theory), and explore intersections to find witnesses for little-o behavior; activity compatible with most graphing calculators.
